name: City life at Liangzhu in the lower Yangtze
summary: Between about 2950 and 2650 BCE people at Liangzhu in the lower Yangtze built a walled city of about 300 hectares with a palace mound, canals and great dams.
description: Earthen walls on a base of quarried rock enclosed the city of Liangzhu, about 300 ha, with the 30 ha Mojiaoshan palatial mound at its centre and some 30 km of moats, ditches and canals controlled by eight water gates. A system of dams and levees to the north was built before most of the city, and a storage pit held 10,000 to 15,000 kg of rice. Most of the city was built between 4,900 and 4,600 cal BP and it had been abandoned by 4,300 to 4,200 BP. UNESCO describes it as the centre of power and belief of an early regional state and an outstanding example of early urban civilization. The later centres named in the lead (Shimao, Taosi, Erlitou) are not part of this record.

impact.note: One early regional state around Lake Tai (reach 1); UNESCO describes a change from small Neolithic societies to a large integrated political unit with hierarchy, which is a new basis for how people were organised (depth 3); the city was abandoned, and what later Chinese centres took from it is not shown in the sources (generativity 1).

date.label: 4,900 to 4,600 cal BP (c. 2950 to 2650 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Most of Liangzhu city was built between 4,900 and 4,600 cal BP, about 2950 to 2650 BCE, after the dams and levees to its north.

evidence.supports: The dating of the dams and levees before 4,800 y B.P. reveals that these features most likely existed before the construction of most of Liangzhu city dated at 4,900–4,600 cal B.P.

date.label: c. 3300 to 2300 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: UNESCO's World Heritage listing dates the building of the City Site at Liangzhu to about 3300 to 2300 BCE.

evidence.supports: With a series of sites, including the City Site built during ca. 3300-2300 BCE, the Peripheral Water Conservancy System with complex functions and socially-graded cemeteries (including an altar)

date.label: by 4,300 to 4,200 years BP (c. 2350 to 2250 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Liangzhu had been abandoned by 4,300 to 4,200 years BP, about 2350 to 2250 BCE.

evidence.supports: eventually many of these cities were rendered unsustainable and were abandoned, as evidently occurred at Liangzhu by 4,300–4,200 y B.P.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The coordinates of Liangzhu are from the supervisor's memory, not from a source; UNESCO's map could not be read. Check against a gazetteer.
UNESCO's c. 3300 to 2300 BCE is the span of the Liangzhu culture as a whole; the radiocarbon range for the city itself (4,900 to 4,600 cal BP) is the anchor.
No population estimate was sourced, and the sources do not argue the case for independence from western Eurasia.
Shimao, Taosi and Erlitou (the lead's later end, c. 1800 BCE) were not checked and need their own records; whether they owed anything to Liangzhu is an open link.

research.note: Neither source discusses whether Liangzhu's builders knew of cities elsewhere; UNESCO treats it as a contribution of the Yangtze basin to the origins of Chinese civilization. The lead's claim of independence from western Eurasia is likely but is not argued in what was read.
